section_summary: This section contains two copies of an Embassy despatch assessing Japan’s debt, proposed military spending, and the risk that further bond issues would cause inflation and weaken the yen. It also includes two copies of a report on negotiations over the City of Tokio’s 1912 loan, a consular letter and clipping about loans to Japanese residents in Southeast Asia, and a January 1937 telegram with a partial paraphrase on Japan’s financial position.

subfiles.title: Japan’s financial position and military spending
subfiles.from: Erle R. Diekover, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Assesses whether Japan can finance military expansion and promised civilian reforms through further bond issues.
subfiles.summary: The despatch compares Japan’s rising national debt with its capacity to absorb deficit bonds. It argues that Army and Navy demands may crowd out civilian reforms. Forcing institutions to buy bonds could accelerate inflation and yen depreciation, although Finance Minister Baba is described as resisting that course.

subfiles.title: Japan’s financial position and military spending, duplicate copy
subfiles.from: Erle R. Diekover, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Responds to a Department request for comment on an article about Japan’s economic choices.
subfiles.summary: This full copy of despatch No. 2030 reviews national debt, planned bond issues, and the proposed 1937–38 budget. It questions whether Japan can fund both defense expansion and social reforms without forcing bond purchases, causing inflation, and weakening the yen.

subfiles.title: City of Tokio Loan 1912
subfiles.from: Edwin C. Wilson, for the Ambassador, U.S. Embassy, Paris
subfiles.about: Reports a proposed settlement between the City of Tokio and French holders of its 1912 loan.
subfiles.summary: Wilson describes the city’s proposed cash and new-bond payments. Bondholders reportedly rejected the offer in its present form, chiefly over the currency of payment, though a representative expected a compromise.

subfiles.title: City of Tokio Loan 1912, duplicate copy
subfiles.from: Edwin C. Wilson, for the Ambassador, U.S. Embassy, Paris
subfiles.about: Duplicates the report on negotiations with French holders of the City of Tokio’s 1912 loan.
subfiles.summary: A second, noisier copy of the despatch on the city’s offer and the bondholders’ response.

subfiles.title: Letter enclosing clipping on Bank of Formosa loans
subfiles.from: Chas. L. Hoover, American Consul General, Hong Kong
subfiles.to: Erle R. Diekover, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a newspaper item on loans to Japanese merchants, farmers, and industrialists in Malaya and the Netherlands Indies.
subfiles.summary: Hoover encloses a South China Morning Post clipping about Bank of Formosa loans.

subfiles.title: Southward Move: Loans to 15,000 Japanese in Malaya and the Netherlands Indies
subfiles.about: Describes Bank of Formosa loans for Japanese residents in Malaya and the Netherlands Indies.
subfiles.summary: Reports loan terms and funds earmarked for Java and Singapore.

subfiles.title: Stray duplicate page on Japan’s financial position
subfiles.from: Erle R. Diekover, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Repeats part of the earlier despatch on military budgets, bond issues, and inflation.
subfiles.summary: A stray, heavily degraded duplicate of material on pages 492–493.

subfiles.title: Japan’s financial situation, telegram No. 5, section one
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reviews Japan’s debt, bond market, trade balance, yen pressure, and new foreign exchange controls.
subfiles.summary: Grew says Japan’s finances are weaker but not yet in serious condition. The enlarged budget will require more deficit bonds, while banks struggle to place existing issues. Rising imports, reduced exchange reserves, and pressure on the yen prompted exchange controls announced on January 8.

subfiles.title: Japan’s financial situation, telegram No. 5, section two
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Evaluates the longer-term effects of Japan’s proposed 1937–38 budget on bond prices and the yen.
subfiles.summary: Observers expect the larger budget and continued deficit financing to strain Japan’s resources. They anticipate credit inflation and rising prices but believe government measures can avert an immediate financial crisis. The Embassy offers to obtain further detail for the Treasury.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of telegram No. 5
subfiles.about: Paraphrases the opening assessment and unfavorable factors from the January 13 telegram.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase restates the debt and reserve figures, weak demand for deficit bonds, the enlarged budget, expected import excess, and pressure on the yen. It continues beyond the final page supplied.
